title: Plant Tissue Traits and Postharvest Quality of Fruit and Vegetable By-Products: An Integrative Review Toward a Zero-Waste Raw-Material Framework for Plant-Based Food Development
content: Fruit and vegetable by-products are postharvest crop-derived tissue fractions whose value for plant-based food development depends on tissue identity, quality history, stabilization readiness, and raw-material specification, rather than on recoverable compounds alone. This integrative review synthesizes tissue-level, postharvest, stabilization, and analytical evidence to clarify how fruit and vegetable by-products can be evaluated as zero-waste raw-material candidates rather than as generic residues or compound sources. We integrate crop source, cultivar or maturity, organ/tissue fraction, postharvest history, and stabilization route to evaluate the quality, safety, reproducibility, and application readiness of fruit and vegetable by-products. Brassicaceae crops, including napa cabbage, radish, cabbage, broccoli, and cauliflower, are used as representative leafy, root, stem, and trimming systems in which tissue fragility, sulfur-containing metabolites, water status, and rapid quality loss are especially relevant. Based on this synthesis, we propose a tissue-to-raw-material framework linking crop and organ identity, tissue segregation, postharvest quality diagnosis, stabilization, analytical fingerprinting, specification setting, and route matching. Through this plant-tissue-centered perspective, zero-waste development is presented as a quality-preserving strategy for assigning crop-derived tissues primarily to plant-based food development and, where evidence supports it, to fermentation substrates, edible coating/film systems, or selected secondary material routes when safety, stability, and specifications are met.
